title: Lipid-State Transduction Framework: A Biological Causal Research Programme for Source-State Continuity, Extracellular Editing, and Route Resolved Function
content: Extracellular lipid biology is already described by mature frameworks for lipoprotein metabolism, extracellular vesicles, membrane biophysics, lipid signaling, and biomolecular coronas. The present article therefore does not propose a new particle taxonomy or a universal mathematical model. Instead, it defines a biological causal research programme for testing whether a source-associated lipid-interface state can remain informative after extracellular release, undergo constrained remodeling and acquisition of a fluid-derived identity, and alter a defined biological route. The framework integrates two previously published hypotheses while separating four biological questions that are often conflated: whether a source condition causally changes the initial lipid interface; whether persistent structural features constrain subsequent remodeling; whether acquired particle-associated material changes the interface, acts directly on recipient pathways, or becomes inseparable from the edited particle; and whether the resulting state changes route-resolved function beyond established mechanisms. Causal interpretation is tied to source intervention, calibrated structural tolerances, orthogonal state measurements, pathway-specific perturbation, and system-specific causal diagrams that distinguish pre-exposure confounders from mediators, downstream consequences, and technical quality-control variables. Confirmatory failure requires prospectively powered, independently prepared replication, while predictive utility is evaluated separately from causal support. History dependence is treated as an exploratory conjecture rather than a core requirement, and the proposed non-classical lipid-state particle remains a high-risk conjecture until positive structural and causal criteria are met. The framework is thus positioned as an empirically unvalidated but falsifiable research programme whose value lies in making extracellular lipid-state claims biologically testable and easier to reject when established explanations are sufficient.
